input.question: What would a distance vs time graph look like for a rocket accelerating from rest to relativistic speeds?
input.ground_truth: I will assume that the object starts from rest at the origin and begins to accelerate in the x-direction with constant proper acceleration a. The equation of motion is: dp/dt = ma = d(ymv)/dt, where y = 1/sqrt(1-(v/c)^(2)) is the Lorentz factor. d(yv)/dt = a yv = at = v/sqrt(1-(v/c)^(2)). Now we want to solve for the velocity as a function of time. (at)^(2)[1 - (v/c)^(2)] = v^(2) (at)^(2) = v^(2)[1 + (at/c)^(2)] v^(2) = (at)^(2)/[1 + (at/c)^(2)] v(t) = at/sqrt[1 + (at/c)^(2)]. Now we want the position as a function of time, so we'll make the change of variables u = at/c, du = (a/c) dt. We want to integrate uc^(2)/[a\*sqrt[1 + u^(2)]] du. This gives x(t) = (c^(2)/a)\*sqrt[1 + u^(2)] + C, or x(t) = (c^(2)/a)\*sqrt[1 + (at/c)^(2)] + C. But we said that it should start at the origin, so that tells us what the constant C should be: C = -c^(2)/a. So: x(t) = (c^(2)/a)[sqrt(1 + (at/c)^(2)) - 1]. [Here](_URL_0_) I have plotted x as a function of t, where t is measured in units of c/a for simplicity.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: What would a distance vs time graph look like for a rocket accelerating from rest to relativistic speeds?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Alright, let’s imagine you have a toy rocket that starts not moving at all (that’s what “from rest” means), and then you make it go faster and faster, almost as fast as light can go (that’s what “relativistic speeds” means).

Now, let’s think about a picture with two lines: one for time (like a clock ticking) and one for how far the rocket has gone.

If the rocket goes at a steady speed (like walking at the same pace), the distance vs time graph would look like a straight line going up at an angle. That’s easy!

But if the rocket starts from rest and then speeds up more and more, at first it doesn’t go very far because it’s not moving fast yet. So the line at the start is almost flat (not going up much). But as the rocket gets faster, it goes farther more quickly, so the line starts to get steeper.

Now, here’s the tricky part because of “relativistic speeds”—when things go almost as fast as light, they can’t go any faster. So as the rocket gets closer and closer to light speed, it takes more and more time and energy to make it go even a little bit faster. So the line on the graph gets steeper, but not as steep as it would if it could keep speeding up forever. It starts to flatten out a little bit as it gets close to light speed.

So, the graph would start almost flat, then get steeper as the rocket speeds up, and then the line gets less steep again as the rocket can’t go much faster.

That’s what the distance vs time graph for a rocket speeding up to almost light speed would look like!
